## The Move: What to Actually Do This Week

Whichever category you’re in, the sequence is largely the same. Do these in order:

1.  **Send a written dispute and demand validation.** Under [15 U.S.C. § 1692g](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=\(title:15%20section:1692g%20edition:prelim\)), if you notify a debt collector in writing within 30 days of first contact that you dispute the debt, the collector must stop all collection activity until they mail you verification of the debt. This buys you time and creates a paper record. Use my free [Debt Validation Letter Generator](https://getoutofdebt.org/243974/debt-validation-letter-generator) to send it correctly.
2.  **Request the original signed instrument.** You have a right to see the actual document you supposedly agreed to — the account application, the promissory note, the signature page. Sometimes what comes back doesn’t match what you remember signing, which matters for both a capacity claim and a forgery claim.
3.  **Pull your medical records for the exact date.** Prescription fill dates, hospital admission and discharge notes, anesthesia records, physician notes about your condition that day or week. This is, per the case law above, the single most persuasive category of evidence for a capacity claim — get it while it’s still available.
4.  **File a complaint with the CFPB** at [consumerfinance.gov/complaint](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/complaint/). The Bureau’s rulemaking on coerced debt has stalled, but the individual complaint portal still routes your complaint directly to the company and requires a response, which creates a record even when it doesn’t force an outcome.
5.  **If your signature isn’t yours, file at [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov)** and use the FCRA block described above.
6.  **Talk to a real attorney before you assume anything.** A capacity, duress, or undue-influence claim is fact-specific and state-specific — this is not a do-it-yourself legal strategy. [NACA](https://www.consumeradvocates.org/findanattorney/) can connect you with a consumer-rights attorney who handles exactly this kind of contract defense. If the more realistic path is putting the whole situation behind you rather than fighting to prove what happened years ago, [NACBA](https://nacba.org) can connect you with a bankruptcy attorney, or you can [talk to Damon Day for free](https://DamonDay.com) about whether that’s the faster, cheaper route for your situation. Damon Day, an independent debt coach and my co-host on the Get Out of Debt Guy podcast, whom you can reach at [DamonDay.com](https://damonday.com) — I receive no payment for this referral.

**Key Takeaway:** A contract signed while impaired or under pressure doesn’t disappear on its own — it’s voidable, not void, and you have to raise it with real evidence: medical records tied to the exact date, the terms of the deal, and the nature of the relationship. Coerced-debt statutes are real but new, narrow, and often don’t cover debt that already exists. Forgery and coercion need different remedies — know which one you actually have. And if the person who pressured you has died, what you owe depends on how the debt was structured (joint account, authorized user, cosigner, community property), not on how the relationship ended.

**Free Tool — Debt Validation Letter Generator:** Being contacted by a debt collector? The free Debt Validation Letter Generator creates a personalized FDCPA validation letter in seconds — forcing the collector to prove the debt is real before they can continue. [**Generate My Letter →**](/debt-validation-letter-generator/)

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I get out of a contract I signed while heavily medicated or sedated?

Possibly, but not automatically. Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 15, a contract signed while you couldn’t understand its nature and consequences — or couldn’t act reasonably regarding it, if the other party had reason to know your condition — is voidable. You have to raise it, and courts generally want medical evidence tied to the exact date, not just your recollection or a description of how you seemed.

### What’s the difference between undue influence and duress?

Duress is an improper threat that leaves you no reasonable choice but to sign. Undue influence is unfair persuasion by someone you’re dependent on or who holds your trust — a caregiver, spouse, or someone with your power of attorney — and it doesn’t require an explicit threat, just sustained exploitation of that relationship. Both make a contract voidable by you, but they’re proven differently.

### Does a coerced-debt law protect me if my state doesn’t have one yet?

Not directly — only about a half-dozen states have enacted coerced-debt statutes so far, and where they exist they’re often narrow (specific relationships, specific dates, sometimes prospective-only for debt incurred after the law took effect). Everyone, in every state, still has the underlying contract-law doctrines — incapacity, duress, and undue influence — available regardless of whether their state has passed a coerced-debt law.

### If the person who pressured me into signing has died, do I still owe the debt?

Their death doesn’t erase the debt or your legal claim against it, but it does remove them as a witness. What you actually owe depends on how the debt was structured: joint account holders remain fully liable, authorized users generally are not, cosigners’ estates can still be pursued, and in community property states a surviving spouse can owe a deceased spouse’s individual debts. Outside those situations, debts are paid from the estate, not by family members personally.

### What’s the difference between forgery and being coerced into signing?

Coercion means it’s genuinely your signature, but you were forced, manipulated, or too impaired to give real consent — the fix is a contract-law claim. Forgery means someone signed your name or used your identity without you ever signing anything — the fix is an identity-theft report through IdentityTheft.gov and an FCRA block with the credit bureaus. Mixing these up sends people down the wrong process for months.

#### The Bottom Line

None of this is automatic, and none of it is quick. But it isn’t hopeless, either — the law does recognize that a signature obtained while you couldn’t understand what you were agreeing to, or while someone else’s pressure replaced your own judgment, is not the same as a signature freely and knowingly given. The evidence just has to exist and has to be gathered, and the sooner you start — while medical records are still reachable and the paper trail is still intact — the stronger your position. If someone you know is dealing with this, send them this page.

_One more thing — everything I share here is based on over 30 years of helping people through exactly this. But my advice is input for your decision, not the decision itself. Capacity, undue influence, duress, and coerced-debt law are all fact-specific and vary a lot by state, and your situation may have details that change the answer. Talk to an attorney licensed in your state before you act. Only you know your full situation._

Multiple outlets that investigated found the authenticity of the underlying 'group chat' is unconfirmed and widely doubted.

Key evidence: Yahoo/Business Insider reporting found the @ashleighjamz account 'first posted only three weeks ago' and 'has only Suno-related posts, with no other photos or videos typical of a personal account' (https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/articles/oreogate-instagram-went-viral-fake-173312243.html). Dexerto reported that 'Suno subsequently confirmed to Business Insider that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners' and that despite questioning, 'ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real,' concluding 'There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated' — i.e., it remains unverified either way (https://www.dexerto.com/food/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real-3403588/). AOL's coverage states plainly: 'There is some talk online that "Oreogate" may not have been a real mom-group meltdown at all. The posts have not been verified as actual conversations, and the music playing was reportedly generated by AI' (https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/articles/oreogate-parents-picking-sides-over-170849551.html). SheKnows ran a piece titled 'Was Oreogate Fake?' directly questioning the story's veracity (https://www.sheknows.com/parenting/articles/1235074192/moms-oreos-was-it-fake/). AOL's own analysis noted 'Almost immediately, internet sleuths were calling out the exchanges as fake,' while also pointing out the account's prior series was literally titled fictional-sounding ('Texts from the worst bachelorette trip of my life') (https://www.aol.com/articles/oreogate-probably-fake-unhinged-mom-192631000.html).

The underlying narrative details the Daily Wire tweet cites (school/teacher refusing the ban, the lunchbox search, and 'Oreo Day') do match what was depicted in the viral Instagram posts — so the tweet's summary is broadly consistent with the viral content as presented. However, the Daily Wire presents this as a real news event/incident without any indication that: (1) it originated as paid advertising content (#sunopartner) for an AI music generation app, and (2) its factual authenticity has never been confirmed and has been seriously questioned by multiple outlets, with the creator declining to confirm the story was real.

This omission is significant because the Daily Wire is treating unverified, AI-generated/sponsored content as a factual anecdote about real parents and a real incident, which readers would reasonably want to know given how widely this was flagged as possibly fabricated or an ad campaign.

# Viral ‘Oreogate’ mom drama was a paid AI ad and its creator won’t say if it was real

A viral Instagram saga about a mother trying to ban Oreos from her daughter’s kindergarten has been confirmed as a paid partnership with an AI company, but its creator has declined to say whether the messages were authentic.

The drama, dubbed “Oreogate,” was shared by Instagram creator ashleighjamz across 13 videos. The [first installment surpassed 10 million views](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMjhWyzFYX/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) as parents, medical creators and brands weighed in on the increasingly bizarre dispute.

Each video presented screenshots from an alleged parent WhatsApp group, with the messages transformed into songs using AI music generator Suno.

The saga began when a mother named Michelle asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, chocolate and candy because her daughter Ava was not allowed to eat them and became upset after seeing another child with the cookies.

Other mothers refused, while the messages claimed Michelle complained to the school, searched children’s lunchboxes and requested that Ava be seated away from classmates eating Oreos. A later installment seemingly revealed that Ava had been trading her own snacks for the forbidden cookies.

Oreo even joined the conversation, writing on its [official Threads account](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_/oreo-gate-was-not-on-my-bingo-card/): “OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card.”

## Suno confirms creator partnership behind Oreogate

Despite being widely discussed as a genuine parent-group dispute, every Oreogate caption included the hashtag #sunopartner.

Suno subsequently confirmed to [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/oreogate-mom-drama-suno-ad-fake-2026-8) that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners. The company said it did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline.

“Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want,” a spokesperson said. Oreo also told the outlet it had no involvement in producing the series.

> View on Threads

However, ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real.

The creator said she had deliberately “not been getting into the specifics” while so many people were following the story. According to Business Insider, she stopped responding after receiving additional questions.

Questions had already been raised about the account by internet-culture writer [Stephanie McNeal](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama), who noted it was less than a month old and contained only sponsored Suno videos.

Those posts follow a similar format, including alleged messages from a disastrous bachelorette trip, an ex-boss and a “delusional” friend, all converted into AI-generated songs. Suno has also been used to create [other viral songs that left listeners questioning their origins](https://www.dexerto.com/tiktok/viral-tiktok-song-i-run-confirmed-ai-its-been-removed-from-spotify-3284524/).

There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated. However, with its creator declining to verify them, it remains unclear whether the saga documented a real dispute, was inspired by one or was created entirely as sponsored entertainment.

### https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/articles/oreogate-instagram-went-viral-fake-173312243.html
# 'Oreogate' on Instagram went viral. But was it all a fake ad for an AI company?

*   "Oreogate" is the latest mom group chat drama over sending kids to lunch with an Oreo.
    
*   The series of viral videos is actually a piece of marketing for Suno, an AI music app.
    
*   But was the story itself even real? We may never know.
    

The situation is relatable to anyone who has been in a parent WhatsApp chat: one person says something ridiculous, and everyone else has to react with varying degrees of politeness or directness. Side chats ensue, tensions start to boil.

Oreogate is a series of viral Instagram posts from user @ashleighjamz about a fight over kindergarteners bringing Oreos for lunch in a classroom group chat, and it hits that exact nerve.

Over 13 videos (so far), the saga unfolds. The mother of "Ava" asks the other parents in the group not to send Oreos in their lunches because Ava isn't allowed to have Oreos. Ava came home upset and asking for Oreos after seeing another girl with one. The other moms refuse to accommodate this unreasonable request and continue sending Oreos. The other children share their cookies with Ava, and the angry mother says she has complained to the teacher. (To get the full experience, you need to watch the videos.)

The series has gone viral, with coverage in the [New York Post,](https://nypost.com/2026/08/25/lifestyle/moms-ridiculous-school-lunch-oreo-request-triggers-backlash/) [AdAge](https://adage.com/brand-marketing/aa-oreo-responds-oreo-gate-drama/), and other news outlets. The first video in the series has over 10 million views. Other creators and brands have been making posts about it. [Pediatricians](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dchb6XqOyhJ/) are weighing. Dozens of moms have posted videos of themselves [shopping](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dcjf10vu1NE/) for Oreos or [packing them in lunches](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dce3f2wSJP-/) in honor of Ava.

But something about Oreogate seems fishy to me.

The premise works because of how outrageous and entitled the one mom is, but what really makes it is the music. Each video has the words from the WhatsApp screenshots set to music as lyrics. The songs are generated by Suno, an AI music app, according to her caption.

## All the videos are a paid partnership with Suno

And if you keep reading the caption, you'll notice all the Oreogate videos also end with #sunopartner.

So, was this all an ad for a generative [AI music app](https://www.businessinsider.com/why-the-music-industry-is-changing-its-tune-on-ai-2025-12?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo)?

Yes. Suno confirmed to Business Insider that @ashleighjamz is one of their paid partners who creates content about Suno for social media.

Suno, however, also said it doesn't control what their partners post in their ads.

"Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want," said a Suno spokesperson. Basically, Suno didn't come up with the idea to make a song about Oreos or parenting — they just had an existing paid arrangement with someone who had the idea on their own.

(For what it's worth, I also asked Oreo if they had any involvement, and they said no.)

But there's a bigger question that's still unanswered: _Was Oreogate even real?_

## Did Oreogate actually happen?

I reached out to @ashleighjamz over Instagram DM to ask. "I've deliberately not been getting into the specifics of the people/messages behind OreoGate while everything is still happening, just because there are so many people following it and discussing it at the moment," she responded.

After I asked several follow-up questions, she went silent.

Here's why I'm skeptical (and I'm [not the only one](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama)) that any of the Oreogate saga ever transpired in real life.

The @ashleighjamz account, which first posted only three weeks ago, has only Suno-related posts, with no other photos or videos typical of a personal account. Her other videos are similar to Oreogate: screenshots of text messages about infuriating social situations, set to Suno-generated music with the #sunopartner hashtag.

She has videos about "Text from the worst bachelorette trip of my life" (an 8-part series), "Messages from my ex-boss I probably should have reported" (3 parts), "Turning my delusional friend's text into a song," and "My husband lost our dog and this is how he told me."

Another, more practical element that makes me question the videos is that it seems unlikely that someone would share authentic screenshots of this situation, names and all (including the kids' names!).

Unfortunately, without hearing more from @ashleighjamz directly, I can't say for sure whether Oreogate is something she experienced firsthand, or if it was inspired by real events, or if it even happened at all.

## Faked "storytimes" are a new trend in ads

There's a new trend in user-generated content marketing where people invent fake "storytime" type posts about enraging social situations involving horrible bosses, toxic mothers-in-law, or cheating husbands. Kate Lindsay wrote about the trend for [Link In Bio](https://www.linkinbio.news/p/storytime-tiktok-secret-ad), a newsletter about digital marketing, and how it's proliferating on TikTok and Instagram.

We're in a moment now where [it's getting hard to tell what's authentic in our feeds anymore](https://www.businessinsider.com/clipping-social-media-tiktok-viral-band-geese-advertising-authentic-fake-2026-4?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo), and the definition of advertising is being stretched in new ways. After several years of seeing influencers tagging or coyly thanking brands in the comments of a photo— actions that are not always clear disclosures, according to the FTC — I think many of us had sort of felt we had a comfortable understanding of what's an ad or not. But with the rise of clipping, which exists in a strange nexus of advertising and content, and new incentives for creators, platforms, and brands… I'm feeling lost. I think I need an Oreo.

# Viral ‘Oreogate’ mom drama was a paid AI ad and its creator won’t say if it was real

A viral Instagram saga about a mother trying to ban Oreos from her daughter’s kindergarten has been confirmed as a paid partnership with an AI company, but its creator has declined to say whether the messages were authentic.

The drama, dubbed “Oreogate,” was shared by Instagram creator ashleighjamz across 13 videos. The [first installment surpassed 10 million views](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMjhWyzFYX/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) as parents, medical creators and brands weighed in on the increasingly bizarre dispute.

Each video presented screenshots from an alleged parent WhatsApp group, with the messages transformed into songs using AI music generator Suno.

The saga began when a mother named Michelle asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, chocolate and candy because her daughter Ava was not allowed to eat them and became upset after seeing another child with the cookies.

Other mothers refused, while the messages claimed Michelle complained to the school, searched children’s lunchboxes and requested that Ava be seated away from classmates eating Oreos. A later installment seemingly revealed that Ava had been trading her own snacks for the forbidden cookies.

Oreo even joined the conversation, writing on its [official Threads account](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_/oreo-gate-was-not-on-my-bingo-card/): “OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card.”

## Suno confirms creator partnership behind Oreogate

Despite being widely discussed as a genuine parent-group dispute, every Oreogate caption included the hashtag #sunopartner.

Suno subsequently confirmed to [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/oreogate-mom-drama-suno-ad-fake-2026-8) that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners. The company said it did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline.

“Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want,” a spokesperson said. Oreo also told the outlet it had no involvement in producing the series.

> View on Threads

However, ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real.

The creator said she had deliberately “not been getting into the specifics” while so many people were following the story. According to Business Insider, she stopped responding after receiving additional questions.

Questions had already been raised about the account by internet-culture writer [Stephanie McNeal](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama), who noted it was less than a month old and contained only sponsored Suno videos.

Those posts follow a similar format, including alleged messages from a disastrous bachelorette trip, an ex-boss and a “delusional” friend, all converted into AI-generated songs. Suno has also been used to create [other viral songs that left listeners questioning their origins](https://www.dexerto.com/tiktok/viral-tiktok-song-i-run-confirmed-ai-its-been-removed-from-spotify-3284524/).

There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated. However, with its creator declining to verify them, it remains unclear whether the saga documented a real dispute, was inspired by one or was created entirely as sponsored entertainment.

### https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/articles/oreogate-instagram-went-viral-fake-173312243.html
# 'Oreogate' on Instagram went viral. But was it all a fake ad for an AI company?

*   "Oreogate" is the latest mom group chat drama over sending kids to lunch with an Oreo.
    
*   The series of viral videos is actually a piece of marketing for Suno, an AI music app.
    
*   But was the story itself even real? We may never know.
    

The situation is relatable to anyone who has been in a parent WhatsApp chat: one person says something ridiculous, and everyone else has to react with varying degrees of politeness or directness. Side chats ensue, tensions start to boil.

Oreogate is a series of viral Instagram posts from user @ashleighjamz about a fight over kindergarteners bringing Oreos for lunch in a classroom group chat, and it hits that exact nerve.

Over 13 videos (so far), the saga unfolds. The mother of "Ava" asks the other parents in the group not to send Oreos in their lunches because Ava isn't allowed to have Oreos. Ava came home upset and asking for Oreos after seeing another girl with one. The other moms refuse to accommodate this unreasonable request and continue sending Oreos. The other children share their cookies with Ava, and the angry mother says she has complained to the teacher. (To get the full experience, you need to watch the videos.)

The series has gone viral, with coverage in the [New York Post,](https://nypost.com/2026/08/25/lifestyle/moms-ridiculous-school-lunch-oreo-request-triggers-backlash/) [AdAge](https://adage.com/brand-marketing/aa-oreo-responds-oreo-gate-drama/), and other news outlets. The first video in the series has over 10 million views. Other creators and brands have been making posts about it. [Pediatricians](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dchb6XqOyhJ/) are weighing. Dozens of moms have posted videos of themselves [shopping](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dcjf10vu1NE/) for Oreos or [packing them in lunches](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dce3f2wSJP-/) in honor of Ava.

But something about Oreogate seems fishy to me.

The premise works because of how outrageous and entitled the one mom is, but what really makes it is the music. Each video has the words from the WhatsApp screenshots set to music as lyrics. The songs are generated by Suno, an AI music app, according to her caption.

## All the videos are a paid partnership with Suno

And if you keep reading the caption, you'll notice all the Oreogate videos also end with #sunopartner.

So, was this all an ad for a generative [AI music app](https://www.businessinsider.com/why-the-music-industry-is-changing-its-tune-on-ai-2025-12?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo)?

Yes. Suno confirmed to Business Insider that @ashleighjamz is one of their paid partners who creates content about Suno for social media.

Suno, however, also said it doesn't control what their partners post in their ads.

"Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want," said a Suno spokesperson. Basically, Suno didn't come up with the idea to make a song about Oreos or parenting — they just had an existing paid arrangement with someone who had the idea on their own.

(For what it's worth, I also asked Oreo if they had any involvement, and they said no.)

But there's a bigger question that's still unanswered: _Was Oreogate even real?_

## Did Oreogate actually happen?

I reached out to @ashleighjamz over Instagram DM to ask. "I've deliberately not been getting into the specifics of the people/messages behind OreoGate while everything is still happening, just because there are so many people following it and discussing it at the moment," she responded.

After I asked several follow-up questions, she went silent.

Here's why I'm skeptical (and I'm [not the only one](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama)) that any of the Oreogate saga ever transpired in real life.

The @ashleighjamz account, which first posted only three weeks ago, has only Suno-related posts, with no other photos or videos typical of a personal account. Her other videos are similar to Oreogate: screenshots of text messages about infuriating social situations, set to Suno-generated music with the #sunopartner hashtag.

She has videos about "Text from the worst bachelorette trip of my life" (an 8-part series), "Messages from my ex-boss I probably should have reported" (3 parts), "Turning my delusional friend's text into a song," and "My husband lost our dog and this is how he told me."

Another, more practical element that makes me question the videos is that it seems unlikely that someone would share authentic screenshots of this situation, names and all (including the kids' names!).

Unfortunately, without hearing more from @ashleighjamz directly, I can't say for sure whether Oreogate is something she experienced firsthand, or if it was inspired by real events, or if it even happened at all.

## Faked "storytimes" are a new trend in ads

There's a new trend in user-generated content marketing where people invent fake "storytime" type posts about enraging social situations involving horrible bosses, toxic mothers-in-law, or cheating husbands. Kate Lindsay wrote about the trend for [Link In Bio](https://www.linkinbio.news/p/storytime-tiktok-secret-ad), a newsletter about digital marketing, and how it's proliferating on TikTok and Instagram.

We're in a moment now where [it's getting hard to tell what's authentic in our feeds anymore](https://www.businessinsider.com/clipping-social-media-tiktok-viral-band-geese-advertising-authentic-fake-2026-4?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo), and the definition of advertising is being stretched in new ways. After several years of seeing influencers tagging or coyly thanking brands in the comments of a photo— actions that are not always clear disclosures, according to the FTC — I think many of us had sort of felt we had a comfortable understanding of what's an ad or not. But with the rise of clipping, which exists in a strange nexus of advertising and content, and new incentives for creators, platforms, and brands… I'm feeling lost. I think I need an Oreo.

# Viral ‘Oreogate’ mom drama was a paid AI ad and its creator won’t say if it was real

A viral Instagram saga about a mother trying to ban Oreos from her daughter’s kindergarten has been confirmed as a paid partnership with an AI company, but its creator has declined to say whether the messages were authentic.

The drama, dubbed “Oreogate,” was shared by Instagram creator ashleighjamz across 13 videos. The [first installment surpassed 10 million views](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMjhWyzFYX/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) as parents, medical creators and brands weighed in on the increasingly bizarre dispute.

Each video presented screenshots from an alleged parent WhatsApp group, with the messages transformed into songs using AI music generator Suno.

The saga began when a mother named Michelle asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, chocolate and candy because her daughter Ava was not allowed to eat them and became upset after seeing another child with the cookies.

Other mothers refused, while the messages claimed Michelle complained to the school, searched children’s lunchboxes and requested that Ava be seated away from classmates eating Oreos. A later installment seemingly revealed that Ava had been trading her own snacks for the forbidden cookies.

Oreo even joined the conversation, writing on its [official Threads account](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_/oreo-gate-was-not-on-my-bingo-card/): “OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card.”

## Suno confirms creator partnership behind Oreogate

Despite being widely discussed as a genuine parent-group dispute, every Oreogate caption included the hashtag #sunopartner.

Suno subsequently confirmed to [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/oreogate-mom-drama-suno-ad-fake-2026-8) that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners. The company said it did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline.

“Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want,” a spokesperson said. Oreo also told the outlet it had no involvement in producing the series.

> View on Threads

However, ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real.

The creator said she had deliberately “not been getting into the specifics” while so many people were following the story. According to Business Insider, she stopped responding after receiving additional questions.

Questions had already been raised about the account by internet-culture writer [Stephanie McNeal](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama), who noted it was less than a month old and contained only sponsored Suno videos.

Those posts follow a similar format, including alleged messages from a disastrous bachelorette trip, an ex-boss and a “delusional” friend, all converted into AI-generated songs. Suno has also been used to create [other viral songs that left listeners questioning their origins](https://www.dexerto.com/tiktok/viral-tiktok-song-i-run-confirmed-ai-its-been-removed-from-spotify-3284524/).

There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated. However, with its creator declining to verify them, it remains unclear whether the saga documented a real dispute, was inspired by one or was created entirely as sponsored entertainment.

### https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/articles/oreogate-instagram-went-viral-fake-173312243.html
# 'Oreogate' on Instagram went viral. But was it all a fake ad for an AI company?

*   "Oreogate" is the latest mom group chat drama over sending kids to lunch with an Oreo.
    
*   The series of viral videos is actually a piece of marketing for Suno, an AI music app.
    
*   But was the story itself even real? We may never know.
    

The situation is relatable to anyone who has been in a parent WhatsApp chat: one person says something ridiculous, and everyone else has to react with varying degrees of politeness or directness. Side chats ensue, tensions start to boil.

Oreogate is a series of viral Instagram posts from user @ashleighjamz about a fight over kindergarteners bringing Oreos for lunch in a classroom group chat, and it hits that exact nerve.

Over 13 videos (so far), the saga unfolds. The mother of "Ava" asks the other parents in the group not to send Oreos in their lunches because Ava isn't allowed to have Oreos. Ava came home upset and asking for Oreos after seeing another girl with one. The other moms refuse to accommodate this unreasonable request and continue sending Oreos. The other children share their cookies with Ava, and the angry mother says she has complained to the teacher. (To get the full experience, you need to watch the videos.)

The series has gone viral, with coverage in the [New York Post,](https://nypost.com/2026/08/25/lifestyle/moms-ridiculous-school-lunch-oreo-request-triggers-backlash/) [AdAge](https://adage.com/brand-marketing/aa-oreo-responds-oreo-gate-drama/), and other news outlets. The first video in the series has over 10 million views. Other creators and brands have been making posts about it. [Pediatricians](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dchb6XqOyhJ/) are weighing. Dozens of moms have posted videos of themselves [shopping](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dcjf10vu1NE/) for Oreos or [packing them in lunches](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dce3f2wSJP-/) in honor of Ava.

But something about Oreogate seems fishy to me.

The premise works because of how outrageous and entitled the one mom is, but what really makes it is the music. Each video has the words from the WhatsApp screenshots set to music as lyrics. The songs are generated by Suno, an AI music app, according to her caption.

## All the videos are a paid partnership with Suno

And if you keep reading the caption, you'll notice all the Oreogate videos also end with #sunopartner.

So, was this all an ad for a generative [AI music app](https://www.businessinsider.com/why-the-music-industry-is-changing-its-tune-on-ai-2025-12?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo)?

Yes. Suno confirmed to Business Insider that @ashleighjamz is one of their paid partners who creates content about Suno for social media.

Suno, however, also said it doesn't control what their partners post in their ads.

"Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want," said a Suno spokesperson. Basically, Suno didn't come up with the idea to make a song about Oreos or parenting — they just had an existing paid arrangement with someone who had the idea on their own.

(For what it's worth, I also asked Oreo if they had any involvement, and they said no.)

But there's a bigger question that's still unanswered: _Was Oreogate even real?_

## Did Oreogate actually happen?

I reached out to @ashleighjamz over Instagram DM to ask. "I've deliberately not been getting into the specifics of the people/messages behind OreoGate while everything is still happening, just because there are so many people following it and discussing it at the moment," she responded.

After I asked several follow-up questions, she went silent.

Here's why I'm skeptical (and I'm [not the only one](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama)) that any of the Oreogate saga ever transpired in real life.

The @ashleighjamz account, which first posted only three weeks ago, has only Suno-related posts, with no other photos or videos typical of a personal account. Her other videos are similar to Oreogate: screenshots of text messages about infuriating social situations, set to Suno-generated music with the #sunopartner hashtag.

She has videos about "Text from the worst bachelorette trip of my life" (an 8-part series), "Messages from my ex-boss I probably should have reported" (3 parts), "Turning my delusional friend's text into a song," and "My husband lost our dog and this is how he told me."

Another, more practical element that makes me question the videos is that it seems unlikely that someone would share authentic screenshots of this situation, names and all (including the kids' names!).

Unfortunately, without hearing more from @ashleighjamz directly, I can't say for sure whether Oreogate is something she experienced firsthand, or if it was inspired by real events, or if it even happened at all.

## Faked "storytimes" are a new trend in ads

There's a new trend in user-generated content marketing where people invent fake "storytime" type posts about enraging social situations involving horrible bosses, toxic mothers-in-law, or cheating husbands. Kate Lindsay wrote about the trend for [Link In Bio](https://www.linkinbio.news/p/storytime-tiktok-secret-ad), a newsletter about digital marketing, and how it's proliferating on TikTok and Instagram.

We're in a moment now where [it's getting hard to tell what's authentic in our feeds anymore](https://www.businessinsider.com/clipping-social-media-tiktok-viral-band-geese-advertising-authentic-fake-2026-4?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=yahoocom&utm_medium=syndication&utm_source=yahoo), and the definition of advertising is being stretched in new ways. After several years of seeing influencers tagging or coyly thanking brands in the comments of a photo— actions that are not always clear disclosures, according to the FTC — I think many of us had sort of felt we had a comfortable understanding of what's an ad or not. But with the rise of clipping, which exists in a strange nexus of advertising and content, and new incentives for creators, platforms, and brands… I'm feeling lost. I think I need an Oreo.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow [Business Insider](https://profiles.yahoo.com/brands/business-insider/) on Yahoo.

# List of Democrats Who Voted Against Bill to ‘Defund the Taliban’

Several Democrats voted against a new bill that the measure's proponents say would claw back U.S. funds that wind up in the hands of the [Taliban](https://www.newsweek.com/trump-admin-criticized-funding-taliban-afghanistan-11182133) weekly.

The No Tax Dollars for Terrorists Act passed the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Thursday, but all Democrats on the committee voted against the legislation.

## Why It Matters

Weekly cash shipments of around $40 million USD have been getting sent to the [Afghanistan Central Bank,](https://www.newsweek.com/united-states-funding-taliban-records-reports-humanitarian-aid-2011720) according to U.S. Representative Tim Burchett, Tennessee Republican, who introduced the bill.

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken also said in December 2024 that around $10 million had been paid to the Taliban in the form of taxes.

![Democratic U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire is pictured during a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on Wednesday in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/GettyImages-2258665595.jpg?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1)

...

## What To Know

The committee's Democrats who voted against passing the new piece of legislation include Senators Jeanne Shaheen (New Hampshire), Chris Coons (Delaware), Chris Murphy (Connecticut), Tim Kaine (Virginia), Jeff Merkley (Oregon), Cory Booker (New Jersey), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (Maryland), Tammy Duckworth (Illinois) and Jacky Rosen (Nevada).

If the new bill becomes law, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be required to produce reports scrutinizing how money flows to the Taliban, purportedly through U.S. foreign-aid channels.

Rubio would also be instructed to create a strategy to "discourage foreign countries and nongovernmental organizations from providing financial or material support to the Taliban."

While the U.S. prohibits direct funding to the Taliban, U.S. taxpayer dollars reportedly reach them indirectly through humanitarian organizations that America works with, and these groups in turn often must pay fees and taxes to the Taliban.

A 2025 SIGAR report found that since the Taliban took over in 2021, $10.72 billion has gone to Afghanistan, with $3.83 billion of that coming directly from U.S. taxpayers. It’s estimated by some that up to 70 percent of that money ended up in the Taliban’s hands.

“The Biden administration sent billions of dollars to places where aid diversion to terrorist groups like the Taliban has been well documented," a spokesperson for the State Department previously told _Newsweek_. "By contrast, President Trump directed the Department to suspend all direct assistance that could reach the hands of the Taliban."

They added: "The Trump Administration will not allow U.S. taxpayer dollars to be used to enable the Taliban’s heinous behavior. We condemn the United Nations for failing to implement adequate safeguards and for allowing international aid flows that risk falling into the hands of terrorists.”

Democratic U.S. Representative Jonathan Jackson of Illinois said last year that the bill had bipartisan support but wanted more transparency from the Trump administration about its position in Afghanistan.

“There is not a consensus about what the Trump administration is doing on Afghanistan, because they won’t tell us,” Jackson said. “We urgently need more information and assurances from the Trump administration about their priorities in Afghanistan and now Iran.”

## What People Are Saying

**Burchett, on X:** “Defund the Taliban bill is up today. $40 million of your money goes to the Taliban every week. Let’s end it.”

**Kentucky Republican U.S. Senator Rand Paul, on X:** “If H.R. 260 becomes law, $631M meant for Afghanistan reconstruction will be clawed back to the Treasury. After twenty years of war and failure, not another dollar should ever reach the Taliban."

**Montana Republican U.S. Senator Tim Sheehy, in a statement:** “There is no justification for a dime of U.S. taxpayer money finding its way into the hands of terrorists who openly call for ‘death to America.’ I’m glad to see the Foreign Relations Committee advance the commonsense No Tax Dollars for Terrorists Act and will keep fighting to get it over the finish line.”

## What Happens Next

The bill would still require wider Senate approval before heading to the president’s desk for full passage.

### https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/
# Did slaves braid maps in cornrows to facilitate escape? History behind the legend

News

## Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

### Published May 16, 2026

For [years](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922), a story that slaves' cornrows hid maps and messages to facilitate their escapes to freedom spread online as the stuff of internet legend. The idealistic story, indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances, mirrors others that seek to show slaves' ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad. 

Examples of the claim appeared on [X](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922) ([archived](https://perma.cc/STM9-QQC7)) and [Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=122178080858200550&set=gm.8283090635117721&idorvanity=1305395626220625) One stated: 

> Cornrows were used during slavery to help slaves escape. Slaves used cornrows to transport and create maps to flee plantations. It is most documented in Colombia where Benkos Bioho, a king captured from Africa by the Portuguese who escaped slavery, built San Basillio de Palenque, a village in Northern Colombia around the 17th century. Bioho created his own language as well as an intelligence network and also came up with the idea to have women create maps and deliver messages through their cornrows.

![](https://mediaproxy.snopes.com/width/600?url=https://media.snopes.com/2026/05/cornrows_repack.png)

**(Facebook page Ancient Theories Nerd)**

Snopes has been receiving reader inquiries about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn't mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

"When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That's the core message and that's true," Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California, Los Angeles, told us.

"\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows ... make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind," she said. 

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. "It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top," Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> "And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape," Asprilla Garcia says. "In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped."
> 
> "Why did they not speak the messages?" someone asks.
> 
> "By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language," Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women's braids "was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape."

The practice of hiding seeds in hair was mentioned in the book "[Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas](https://books.google.com.pr/books?id=YXWkwXHFWf0C&printsec=frontcover&dq=%22The+African+Origins+of+Rice+Cultivation+in+the+Americas%22&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=hair&f=false)," by Judith Carney, a professor of geography at UCLA. She wrote about the possible African origins of a rice found in the South American country of Suriname:

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. In the area of Cayenne where a French agronomist found the Baga varieties, the Djuka maroons maintain that rice originally came from Africa, brought by female slaves who smuggled in their hair grains from the slave ships that transported them to the New World. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.   
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors' hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom. 

The use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point. 

Even without proof of its authenticity, Turner says the practice made some sense in the U.S. "People felt Black bodies belonged to them. If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. The possibility that at some point someone may have hid something in their hair, I can't argue against ... because it does adhere to some kind of logic at the time," she said. 

While there is not a lot of definitive research out there about cornrows, historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction. Historian Fergus M. Bordewich wrote in a [New York Times](https://web.archive.org/web/20210317115330/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html) opinion piece in 2007:

> Few aspects of the American past have inspired more colorful mythology than the Underground Railroad. It's probably fair to say that most Americans view it as a thrilling tapestry of midnight flights, hairbreadth escapes, mysterious codes and strange hiding places.
> 
> So it's not surprising that the intriguing (if only recently invented) tale of escape maps encoded in antebellum quilts — enshrined in a metastasizing library of children's books and teachers' lesson plans and perhaps even in a Central Park memorial to Frederick Douglass — should also seize the popular imagination.

In her book, "[Crafted Lives: Stories and Studies of African-American Quilters](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crafted_Lives_Stories_and_Studies_of_Afr/dfaPC_WSlNwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=railroad)," Turner interrogates the mythology around the quilts, and points out that they grew popular from children's stories and oral history. In the 90s book, "Sweet Clara and the Freedom Quilt," a young slave uses scraps of cloth to fashion a map on a quilt, something her master would never recognize. 

We prodded Turner further on whether we could definitively answer the question posed in this article, but she preferred to focus on the attention that legends like this brought to the real stories of the resilience of Black slaves. "I am reticent to say anything too concrete, because I want lay people to want to know more about what life was like for enslaved people," she responded. "There is no real value added to harshly saying 'no' to a story." 

"You can couch your language \[and say\] 'Well, no slave narrative covers it.' Others will say, 'Well that doesn't mean it didn't happen,'" she continued. 

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if 'mainstream culture' was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

While we cannot definitively answer the question of whether this was a real practice by slaves fleeing captivity in the American South, we can point to the rich and varied tales surrounding a real movement toward emancipation. Those stories certainly matter to people, hence their continuing popularity today. 

_Additional reporting by Jordan Liles._

#### Sources

Brown, DeNeen. "Afro-Colombian Women Braid Messages of Freedom in Hairstyles." Washington Post, 8 July 2011. www.washingtonpost.com, https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/afro-colombian-women-braid-messages-of-freedom-in-hairstyles/2011/07/08/gIQA6X9W4H\_story.html.

### [By Nur Ibrahim](/author/nuribrahim/)

Nur Nasreen Ibrahim is a reporter with experience working in television, international news coverage, fact checking, and creative writing.

### https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/
# Did Slaves Braid Routes to Freedom Into Hairstyles? – Truth or Fiction?

In February 2019, a Facebook user shared a [post](https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?fbid=10205332975439984&set=a.1879870452590&type=3&theater) ([archived here](https://archive.fo/tmxEA)) that showed patterns for hairstyles with a claim that slaves used braid patterns to plot out routes to freedom:

> What if I told you all, during slavery, our ancestors braided escape route patterns in their hairstyles too flee bondage and seek freedom from their oppessors! #BlackHistory365

The claim itself did not originate with the February 2019 Facebook post above. A July 2018 thread on the Reddit sub r/IsItBullshit queried fellow redditors about the same rumor:

In that post, the original poster raised questions about the feasibility of such a strategy and asked how braids could functionally be used as maps. In the comments, other users pointed out a presence of initial search results for the claim but a dearth of authoritative sources to support it. One prominent result was from a [blog](https://face2faceafrica.com/article/how-cornrows-were-used-as-an-escape-map-from-slavery-across-south-america), which appeared to repeat anecdotal stories about the use of such a practice in South Africa, as did [another](https://blackdoctor.org/508605/history-of-african-hair-braiding/) with a related folk claim — that grain was secreted in braids.

One example of the way the claim presented appeared in a June 2016 HelloBeautiful.com [article](https://hellobeautiful.com/2877570/braids-cornrows-maps-for-slaves/):

> Writing (if they even possessed that skill) or drawing out the map could lead to them being discovered and then most likely sold again, or killed out of anger from their master. How could they move and plan covertly with minimal risk of being discovered? The women would weave the maps in their hair, carving out paths with their cornrows. Some patterns were even utilized to deliver secret messages.

A June 2018 _Essence_ [article](https://www.essence.com/hair/respect-our-roots-brief-history-our-braids-cultural-appropriation/) also relied on anecdotal claims:

> “\[Hairstyles needed to\] last an entire week.” Without time, resources or products, African-American women took to wearing their tresses in a more simplistic fashion. The women chose easier-to-manage styles, like single plaits, and used oils they had on hand, such as kerosene, to condition them. Braids also served another purpose: They became a secret messaging system for slaves to communicate with one another underneath their masters’ noses. \[Lori L. Tharps, an associate professor at Temple -University\] explains that “people would use braids as a map to freedom.” For instance, the number of plaits worn could indicate how many roads people needed to walk or where to meet someone to escape bondage.

One of the earliest mentions online of related claims was in a 2011 _Washington Post_ [piece](https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/afro-colombian-women-braid-messages-of-freedom-in-hairstyles/2011/07/08/gIQA6X9W4H_story.html?utm_term=.361bf64bc666), “Afro-Colombian women braid messages of freedom in hairstyles.” In it, a woman named Ziomara Asprilla Garcia discussed the oral history of braiding at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Colombia:

> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. “It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top,” Asprilla Garcia says. Someone in the crowd tells Asprilla Garcia that style seems very much like the one she sees black women in the District wearing. “Yes, also,” she says. “And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape,” Asprilla Garcia says. “In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped.” “Why did they not speak the messages?” someone asks. “By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language,” Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women’s braids “was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape.” Not every woman who was planning to escape had the same braids. “Always,” Asprilla Garcia says, “there was a big mother in the whole group.” Such matriarchs always had a distinctive hairstyle. “The rest would know what it meant.”

In 2017, a _New York Times Magazine_ [item](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/12/t-magazine/fashion/braids-hair-beauty.html) about the history of braid patterns describes the claim as a “legend” — not necessarily untrue, but still unproven:

> The practice of braiding hair is truly ancient and culturally universal, dating back at least to 3000 B.C. If hairstyles have traditionally conveyed messages — about standards of beauty, identity, socioeconomic status — braids may be the ultimate example. In republican Rome, wealthy women wore their hair long and braided while slaves were often made to cut theirs short. Ironically, legend has it that in South America, cornrows were used as intricate, hiding-in-plain-sight maps to guide escaping African slaves to freedom.

Most sources place the folk claims in countries outside the United States, primarily Colombia and South Africa. The claim is also not without folkloric precedent, bearing close resemblance to a similar story about coded quilts circulating in the American South since the Civil War era. In a 2007 _TIME_ article about the existence of “[quilt codes](http://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html)” and purported use during the Underground Railroad, scholars debated the plausibility of such stories. As one museum coordinator explained, much of the living history of slaves was not recorded properly:

> But women like Anna Lopez, the education coordinator at the Plymouth Historical Museum, see no reason why the story of quilt codes can’t be fact. “What I tell kids is, who writes history? Men do. Mostly white men. Then I ask, who made quilts? Women did, and a lot of black women made quilts and passed on their oral history. No one wrote down their history, so who knows?”

Another expert quoted in the piece described how such claims are folkloric antidotes to the harsh brutality of the same history. Another added that in both respects, sorting fact from folklore was nearly impossible:

> Roland Freeman, a civil rights activist and photographer who has been documenting African American quilters for nearly 30 years, has another take on why the story is so popular. “Hidden in Plain View is how we got over those white folks. Right under the nose of white folk we’re sending signs and symbols and they didn’t know it. While I think it’s so ridiculous, African Americans are starved for those kind of stories in our culture and we’re willing to accept it because it’s what we want to hear.” Folklorist and quilt historian Laurel Horton, who has lectured and published papers about the quilt code, says she’s given up on trying to debunk the myth. Instead, she says she’s more interested on focusing on why the story continues to persist. “This whole issue made me realize it’s not a matter of one group having the truth and another not. It’s matter of two different sets of beliefs. It’s made me realize that belief doesn’t have a lot to do with factual representation. People feel in their gut that it’s true so no one can convince them in their head that it’s otherwise.”

Stories of slavery escape routes plotted in both braid patterns and quilts have long circulated in areas where slave trades once flourished. A vacuum of historical record documenting the experience of those enslaved has been filled with oral histories of heroism and great personal risk during a particularly brutal time in American history. Historians remain divided on the authenticity of such claims; their popularity persists.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim in the post is a widely circulated piece of internet folklore about cornrows being used by slaves to create escape maps and hide food/seeds. Snopes investigated this story twice (2022 and again in May 2026, coinciding closely with this tweet's posting date) and found it to be unverified legend rather than confirmed history. Snopes states: 'We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn't mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Folklorist Patricia Turner (UCLA) is quoted saying these are 'kind of urban legends that [serve a] function of giving particulars to generalities' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Truthorfiction.com similarly concluded 'Historians remain divided on the authenticity of such claims; their popularity persists' (https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/), comparing it to the similarly unverified 'quilt code' Underground Railroad legend.

The most commonly cited origin for the story is Benkos Biohó, a 17th-century Colombian Maroon leader who founded San Basilio de Palenque. Wikipedia's entry on Biohó notes this is largely folkloric: 'while there is no direct relationship between him and the municipality of San Basilio de Palenque, contemporary literary culture has led to the belief that he was the founder of the town, though this is inaccurate' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benkos_Bioh%C3%B3). The Wikipedia Cornrows article itself frames this as folklore, not fact: 'According to Black folklore, cornrows were often used to communicate on the Underground Railroad and by Benkos Biohó during his time as a slave in Colombia' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornrows).

Support for the claim mostly rests on oral history from Afro-Colombian communities (e.g., a 2011 Washington Post feature on hair braider Ziomara Asprilla Garcia) and one academic paper based on tour-guide testimony at Elmina Castle in Ghana, not on direct historical/archival evidence from the era of American slavery. The Ancient Origins article notes 'it's hard to say since official history has usually been told by white men and a form of resistance amongst the African diaspora by definition lacks archival evidence' (https://www.ancient-origins.net/weird-facts/braids-0017595).

In short, this is a popular but historically unverified legend — not a confirmed fact — that fact-checkers have been unable to substantiate with primary historical evidence, particularly regarding American slavery specifically.

## Context
Current date (UTC): 2026-10-19T08:36:18.103Z

## Claims to verify
1. The idea that cornrows were used to convey messages by enslaved people is a widely shared legend.
2. There is no documented historical evidence for the use of cornrows to convey messages by enslaved people.
3. Snopes investigated the claim and found no tangible evidence of enslaved people in the U.S. using cornrows to convey messages.
4. The more documented version of the cornrows messaging story is tied to 17th-century Colombia.
5. The documented version of the cornrows messaging story is not tied to U.S. slavery.

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/
# Did slaves braid maps in cornrows to facilitate escape? History behind the legend

News

## Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

### Published May 16, 2026

For [years](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922), a story that slaves' cornrows hid maps and messages to facilitate their escapes to freedom spread online as the stuff of internet legend. The idealistic story, indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances, mirrors others that seek to show slaves' ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad. 

Examples of the claim appeared on [X](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922) ([archived](https://perma.cc/STM9-QQC7)) and [Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=122178080858200550&set=gm.8283090635117721&idorvanity=1305395626220625) One stated: 

> Cornrows were used during slavery to help slaves escape. Slaves used cornrows to transport and create maps to flee plantations. It is most documented in Colombia where Benkos Bioho, a king captured from Africa by the Portuguese who escaped slavery, built San Basillio de Palenque, a village in Northern Colombia around the 17th century. Bioho created his own language as well as an intelligence network and also came up with the idea to have women create maps and deliver messages through their cornrows.

![](https://mediaproxy.snopes.com/width/600?url=https://media.snopes.com/2026/05/cornrows_repack.png)

**(Facebook page Ancient Theories Nerd)**

Snopes has been receiving reader inquiries about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn't mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

"When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That's the core message and that's true," Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California, Los Angeles, told us.

"\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows ... make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind," she said. 

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. "It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top," Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> "And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape," Asprilla Garcia says. "In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped."
> 
> "Why did they not speak the messages?" someone asks.
> 
> "By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language," Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women's braids "was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape."

The practice of hiding seeds in hair was mentioned in the book "[Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas](https://books.google.com.pr/books?id=YXWkwXHFWf0C&printsec=frontcover&dq=%22The+African+Origins+of+Rice+Cultivation+in+the+Americas%22&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=hair&f=false)," by Judith Carney, a professor of geography at UCLA. She wrote about the possible African origins of a rice found in the South American country of Suriname:

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. In the area of Cayenne where a French agronomist found the Baga varieties, the Djuka maroons maintain that rice originally came from Africa, brought by female slaves who smuggled in their hair grains from the slave ships that transported them to the New World. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.   
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors' hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom. 

The use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point. 

Even without proof of its authenticity, Turner says the practice made some sense in the U.S. "People felt Black bodies belonged to them. If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. The possibility that at some point someone may have hid something in their hair, I can't argue against ... because it does adhere to some kind of logic at the time," she said. 

While there is not a lot of definitive research out there about cornrows, historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction. Historian Fergus M. Bordewich wrote in a [New York Times](https://web.archive.org/web/20210317115330/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html) opinion piece in 2007:

> Few aspects of the American past have inspired more colorful mythology than the Underground Railroad. It's probably fair to say that most Americans view it as a thrilling tapestry of midnight flights, hairbreadth escapes, mysterious codes and strange hiding places.
> 
> So it's not surprising that the intriguing (if only recently invented) tale of escape maps encoded in antebellum quilts — enshrined in a metastasizing library of children's books and teachers' lesson plans and perhaps even in a Central Park memorial to Frederick Douglass — should also seize the popular imagination.

In her book, "[Crafted Lives: Stories and Studies of African-American Quilters](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crafted_Lives_Stories_and_Studies_of_Afr/dfaPC_WSlNwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=railroad)," Turner interrogates the mythology around the quilts, and points out that they grew popular from children's stories and oral history. In the 90s book, "Sweet Clara and the Freedom Quilt," a young slave uses scraps of cloth to fashion a map on a quilt, something her master would never recognize. 

We prodded Turner further on whether we could definitively answer the question posed in this article, but she preferred to focus on the attention that legends like this brought to the real stories of the resilience of Black slaves. "I am reticent to say anything too concrete, because I want lay people to want to know more about what life was like for enslaved people," she responded. "There is no real value added to harshly saying 'no' to a story." 

"You can couch your language \[and say\] 'Well, no slave narrative covers it.' Others will say, 'Well that doesn't mean it didn't happen,'" she continued. 

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if 'mainstream culture' was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

While we cannot definitively answer the question of whether this was a real practice by slaves fleeing captivity in the American South, we can point to the rich and varied tales surrounding a real movement toward emancipation. Those stories certainly matter to people, hence their continuing popularity today. 

_Additional reporting by Jordan Liles._

#### Sources

Bordewich, Fergus M. "Opinion | History's Tangled Threads." The New York Times, 2 Feb. 2007. NYTimes.com, https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html.

Brown, DeNeen. "Afro-Colombian Women Braid Messages of Freedom in Hairstyles." Washington Post, 8 July 2011. www.washingtonpost.com, https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/afro-colombian-women-braid-messages-of-freedom-in-hairstyles/2011/07/08/gIQA6X9W4H\_story.html.

Carney, Judith A. Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas. Harvard University Press, 2002.

"Did Maps in Cornrows Help Black Slaves Escape Slavery?" Snopes.Com, https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/cornrows-maps-slaves/. Accessed 8 Mar. 2022.

"Juneteenth Marks When Slaves Were Freed." Snopes.Com, https://www.snopes.com/ap/2020/06/18/juneteenth-marks-when-slaves-were-freed/. Accessed 8 Mar. 2022.

Stukin, Stacie. "Breaking News, Analysis, Politics, Blogs, News Photos, Video, Tech Reviews." Time, Apr. 2007. content.time.com,https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html.
